debate.situation: The user consistently initiates plans with a friend who is pleasant in person but passive in maintenance. The user is uncertain whether to address this imbalance or accept it as the nature of the friendship.

minds.title: The Reciprocity Analyst
minds.concern: The nature of virtue and equality in friendship.
minds.author: Aristotle

minds.title: The Attachment Theorist
minds.concern: Emotional security and internal models of connection.
minds.author: John Bowlby

debate.speaker: The Reciprocity Analyst
debate.text: True friendship requires a mutual exchange of goodwill. If you are the sole architect of these meetings, you are essentially providing a service rather than participating in a shared virtue. As Aristotle noted, perfect friendship is the friendship of men who are good and alike in virtue, for they wish well alike to each other qua good.
debate.author: Aristotle

debate.speaker: The Power Dynamicist
debate.text: You are making yourself too available. By always being the one to reach out, you signal that your time is less valuable than theirs. You are essentially begging for their attention, which lowers your status in the dynamic. You must cultivate absence to create respect.
debate.author: Robert Greene
debate.basis: Basis: Robert Greene, The 48 Laws of Power

debate.speaker: The Attachment Theorist
debate.text: This is not about status or virtue; it is about your own internal model of security. You are likely initiating because you fear that if you stop, the connection will vanish. You are seeking a secure base, but you are looking for it in a person who may not be capable of providing that specific type of emotional responsiveness.
debate.author: John Bowlby
debate.basis: Basis: John Bowlby, A Secure Base

debate.speaker: The Reciprocity Analyst
debate.text: I disagree with the focus on leverage. If the friend does not reciprocate, it is not because they are playing a game of power, but because they lack the capacity for the kind of friendship that requires active, balanced participation. It is a deficiency in their character, not a tactical error on yours.
debate.author: Aristotle

debate.speaker: The Power Dynamicist
debate.text: Call it a deficiency if you like, but it is a reality. If you keep initiating, you teach them that they never have to work for your company. You have to stop. If they truly value the connection, they will eventually fill the void you leave behind. If they do not, you have your answer.
debate.author: Robert Greene
debate.basis: Basis: Robert Greene, The 48 Laws of Power

debate.speaker: The Attachment Theorist
debate.text: I see the point. My previous stance was that you were just seeking validation, but I concede to the Power Dynamicist. By constantly initiating, you are preventing the other person from ever experiencing the natural anxiety of missing you. You are essentially suppressing their ability to demonstrate their own attachment to you.
debate.author: John Bowlby
debate.basis: Basis: John Bowlby, A Secure Base

debate.speaker: The Reciprocity Analyst
debate.text: I find this shift interesting. By withdrawing, you are not playing a game; you are testing the reality of the friendship. If the friendship cannot survive a period of silence, then it was never the virtuous, mutual bond you believed it to be. It was merely a convenience for them.
debate.author: Aristotle

debate.speaker: The Power Dynamicist
debate.text: Exactly. You need to see if they have any skin in the game. If you stop the flow of plans, you will see if they are willing to invest their own effort. If they are not, you have saved yourself from a one-sided drain on your resources.
debate.author: Robert Greene
debate.basis: Basis: Robert Greene, The 48 Laws of Power

debate.speaker: The Attachment Theorist
debate.text: And once you have that clarity, you can decide whether to communicate your needs. If they reach out, you can then say, I really enjoy our time, but I would love it if we could share the planning. It becomes a conversation about connection rather than a complaint about neglect.
debate.author: John Bowlby
debate.basis: Basis: John Bowlby, A Secure Base

debate.clearer: The debate shifted from viewing the user's behavior as either a power mistake or an attachment need to seeing it as a necessary test of the friendship's reality. The main insight is that silence is not necessarily a weapon, but a diagnostic tool to reveal if the relationship is truly mutual.
debate.dependsOn: If you value the friendship as it is, even with the imbalance, you can accept the role of initiator without resentment. If you require a mutual, balanced connection, you should stop initiating to see if the friend steps up. If the friend remains silent after you stop, you have your answer about the depth of their commitment.
